Agnes Richter's hand-sewn jacket resides in a museum in Heidelberg. It is covered with an “intricate text [that was] embroidered in five colors over practically every inch of the garment,” (p. ix) circa 1895. Why

268

is it in a museum? It was collected by Heinz Prinzhorn, an art historian who trained as a psychiatrist (but never practiced) who “had a special interest in creativity and madness … and was committed to understanding the expressive impulse in its purest form” (p. x).

For Gail Hornstein, author of Agnes's Jacket: A Psychologist's Search for the Meanings of Madness, the jacket “precisely captures the fundamental conundrum of madness, an experience rich with symbolic meanings that are indecipherable by ordinary means” (p. xi).

Agnes's Jacket, among other things, is an ethnographic study of self-help groups for individuals who experience auditory hallucinations. It is written in the tradition of earlier psychiatrists like R. D. Laing and Thomas Szasz who sought to find meaning in what is conventionally regarded as meaningless insanity.

Hornstein positions herself as an opponent of pharmacological interventions for psychosis, asserting that “in the United States, psychiatry is entirely controlled by doctors, who have a direct economic interest in siding with the drug companies and preventing patients from treating themselves” (p. 53). In Hornstein's view, there is no scientific evidence demonstrating that any pharmacological interventions work.

As a result of her research, Hornstein believes hearing voices is often adaptive, and therefore natural and normal for those who hallucinate. She believes hearing voices is most likely caused by early trauma, and that “[s]exual abuse is, by far, the trauma most frequently found to precede voice hearing … [which] occurred most often when the trauma took place before the age of seven” (p. 41). Hornstein, who attended innumerable support groups both overseas and in the United States, summarizes her ethnographic research:

It took three more years of attending these kinds of meetings, visiting support groups across England, and reading hundreds of pages of materials produced by Hearing Voices Network (HVN) before I felt confident that I understood how hearing voices groups work. … The structure of local HVN groups varies a great deal: Some have fixed membership, while others operate as drop-ins. Some are facilitated by nurses, social workers or occupational therapists; others are run entirely by voice-hearers themselves. HVN meetings are never as tightly structured as those of twelve-step groups like Alcoholics Anonymous, where there's a fixed order and everyone knows exactly what will happen. But all HVN meetings do share certain general themes.

Frank Lachmann is a self-psychologist who brings his scholarly voice to the seminal work of Heinz Kohut. In this volume he seeks to enlarge Kohut's contribution by taking it “from an era of theorizing in which one way influence models predominated, into a theory where transformation is bidirectional and co-created by therapist and patient” (p. 11). In the process, Lachmann makes a strong case for the inherently relational nature of therapeutic change, without departing from his self-psychological roots.

Lachmann evenhandedly integrates findings from the past three decades of systematic infant research with in-depth, psychoanalytic case studies, the specificity and individuality of which drive his unique and complex insights.

The author's direct and humorous voice is engaging from the start, and reflects the clinical approach he advocates. He anticipates, for instance, an understandable reaction to this book as “Oh, no! Not another book about narcissism” so that the reader feels understood. The truth is, however, that this book is about narcissism only in the broadest sense, that is, as one developmental substrate of the development of the self. Indeed, Lachmann aims to offer a perspective on development and treatment that picks up where Kohut's theory of narcissism leaves off.

The book's ostensible theme reflects Kohut's paper, “Forms and Transformations of Narcissism” (1966), in which he suggested that archaic narcissism is transformed either in the course of development, or through treatment into empathy, humor, creativity, an acceptance of transience, and wisdom (p. 257). As Lachmann's text proceeds, each of these traits is taken up in its turn, as the author considers what level of change might be expected in treatment, and how it might be reached.

On the cover of the book is an empty chair and an empty psychoanalytic couch. Who's not there? How can there be a psychotherapy without the self? Opening the book reveals the development over the past 20 years of Epstein's thinking about these matters. In this republication of scholarly papers too long languishing in dusty journals, he reflects,

272

“In my experience, therapy and meditation, psychological development and spiritual realization, seem to be intertwined. One can facilitate the other, or retard the other, or subtly infuse or contaminate the other” (p. 16). What he forcefully contributes to through these papers (and his other books) is an ongoing integration of psychodynamic psychotherapy and the mindfulness of the Buddha. Where psychoanalysis a hundred years ago was digging for some certain truth as to Who I Am, here we find today a different model, one of multiplicity of self, a model of opening and possibility, where “I” is recognized as a passing though useful thought, where the experience of becoming more fully human realizes “thoughts without a thinker.” Epstein's (1995) breakthrough book of the same title established for Buddhism a permanent place at the contemporary psychoanalytic table (where the conversation is not always decorous). These essays reveal the seeds of that book and others, and in themselves, through recurrent themes and considerations, amplify the interrelatedness of psychological and spiritual growth.

The first essays, grouped under “Buddha,” represent Epstein's early attempts to apply what he had learned from his psychiatric residency to the Buddhist studies and meditative experience he had begun as an undergraduate. He starts with narcissism, that pathological investment in self which typifies our culture. Countering the argument that one must have a cohesive self (via ego development) in order to lose a self (via subsequent spiritual growth), he sees meditation “as a vehicle for freeing an individual from his own narcissism, a liberation that is not complete until the experience of enlightenment” (p. 38). Narcissism lingers. The meditative vehicle can hit self-important potholes on the path, as when concentrative rapture masquerades as enlightenment, or when raw terror prevents the contemplation of dissolving self. Meditation in itself, he holds, is neither therapeutic nor nontherapeutic. Like psychoanalysis, it invites the practitioner to take one's own experience as the object of awareness. When the subject ego takes itself as object, “separation of subject and object tends to come undone; the ‘watcher’ dissolves into the dynamic flow” (p. 84) where there is neither self nor no-self. Self becomes nebulous in the mirror of self-reflection. Self-consciousness succumbs to bare awareness of the permeability of arising and passing away. The ego is neither transcended nor repudiated, but seen through: a relative representation with no inherent existence.

In a Series of Conferences, German and Israeli psychoanalysts met with Tavistock-trained group leaders to explore how feelings and fantasies about “German-ness” and “Israeli-ness/Jewish-ness” influenced the ways they related to each other. What do we each believe is the extent, and the limit, of individual responsibility? In our hearts, do we hold ourselves, and each other, accountable for only our own actions and inactions? Survivors Evoke Awe, admiration, and empathy for their triumph over the unbearable. Survivorship provides an identity and path for organizing personal narratives of affliction experienced by family members and friends of eating-disordered persons. The pun in the title of the review of Surviving an Eating Disorder reflects the endemic boundary confusion within this population. It is not only the identified patient, but those around her, who are challenged and must survive. Therefore, the responses and psychological well-being of survivors are essential to the healing process.

Within these pages, those who care for and about a person with an eating disorder will discover that there is no one-size-fits-all model for the treatment of anorexia, bulimia, and overeating. Readers are cautioned that helping someone with these conditions requires tremendous outside support. Survivors learn that they are both part of a common group experience, but also that individualized plans are useful, drawing from the many treatment options available. In this third edition, the late psychotherapist Michele Siegel continues to be credited for providing the book's initial inspiration. The book has been updated with contributions from co-authors Judith Brisman (psychologist/psychoanalyst) and Margot Weinshel (family therapist). Together they offer a comprehensive integration, advocating for the value of psychological inquiry that may be conducive to a psychoanalytic approach over time.

When I was in graduate school studying to be a cognitive psychologist, my fellow students and I were forbidden to use the words “conscious” or, worse yet, “unconscious,” even though, at its inception, experimental psychology averred that a critical concern of the field was the content of consciousness. As experimental psychology rejected the study of the unconscious—indeed, of mental life in general—psychoanalysis remained true to its founder's call that its comprehension was critical to understanding human behavior. If you like, psychoanalysis held the fort while troops of experimental psychologists wandered lost in the forest. They turned their attention to behavior, certain that principles of stimulus-response (S-R) contingencies were sufficient for a complete psychology. It took decades for the field to realize that S-R contingencies could never fully explain language, memory, thinking, and feeling, or to develop an alternative, cognitive psychology. In his new book, What We Don't Know We Know, Ken Eisold observes that because experimental psychologists are no longer only interested in simple acts of perception or motor action, but also in the area in which psychoanalysts are expert—the role unconscious emotions, motives, goals, and implicit memories—the two fields have much to share and gain from one another.

The irony is that just as experimental psychologists rediscovered the unconscious, the field of psychoanalysis began to face problems, both as a professional field and as an academic discipline. Eisold tells the now familiar story: Psychoanalysis has fallen from its once dominant position in psychiatry and psychology.

This article is intended to show the value, limitations, and major concerns in providing psychotherapy and counseling for college and university students. The challenges of the college years, the evolution of campus services, cultural changes affecting postsecondary education, and types of services are noted. Critical issues affecting college mental-health care are discussed, with an emphasis on ethics, effectiveness, and legal issues with suicidal and homicidal threats to life, mandatory treatment, and illicit and prescribed psychotropic drug use.

Interpersonal psychoanalysis, college counseling, college student, detailed inquiry, participant observation, Interpersonal strategies

College students can be difficult to engage in intensive psychodynamic treatment. They focus on external problems, largely eschewing more internally directed, exploratory, insight-oriented work in favor of seeking solutions in the “real world.” Interpersonal psychoanalysis offers strategies that can be employed by therapists from diverse orientations to help college students engage in meaningful dynamic therapy. These strategies are not well known or fully appreciated by many therapists working with college students. In particular, the degree of flexibility inherent to the Interpersonal approach may not be well understood. As an aid to understanding, I elaborate two specific Interpersonal strategies: the detailed inquiry and participant observation. Clinical examples are offered to demonstrate the utility of this approach in engaging college students in more intensive psychotherapy.

In the history of psychoanalysis there has been no shortage of examples of the nasty business that can go on between people, illustrating Harry Stack Sullivan's (1953) maxim that “everyone is much more simply human than otherwise” (p. 32). Louis Breger's fine book helps further the ongoing project of humanizing Sigmund Freud's genius, while offering a richly rendered portrayal of some of the “more simply human” central characters and events that gave rise to the invention of our “impossible profession” (Freud, 1937, p. 247).

In this engaging narrative, written in a lively and accessible style, Breger takes the reader on a journey through the founding of psychoanalysis. Although one must be mindful of the well-established limitations of what might be considered an armchair psychoanalysis (Kuriloff, 2010, personal communication), Breger nonetheless makes a compelling case that Freud, driven by a near-insatiable need for fame and recognition, radically downplayed the role of his mentor and sometime benefactor Josef Breuer.

What is a boy? And what does it mean to have a boyhood in 2010? Does a boy grow psychologically by separating from his mother or by identifying with his father? In his recent book, Boyhoods: Rethinking Masculinities, Ken Corbett tackles these questions. As stated, his premise is that “No two boys, no two boyhoods are the same” (p. 3).

Corbett's Boyhoods essentially comprises an anthology of his psychoanalytic essays written between 2001 and 2009. The essays develop his progressive theoretical psychoanalysis of boyhoods and an evolving, multifaceted conception of gender. In the final chapter, “Fantastic Phallicism: Recognition, Relation, and Phallic Narcissism,” Corbett adds some provocative concepts to his body of work.

Corbett sets out to “capture the lives of boys, in particular the movement, the friendships, and the multiple eroticism that informs boys' lives” (p. 2). Boys, he contends, “collect as a pattern—as Walt Whitman might have it, every one disintegrated yet part of the scheme” (p. 3). In his view, “a kind of ‘Phallophobia’ has crept into our cultural theorizing” (p. 218), with the male body and the positive valence of phallic aggression disavowed (p. 219). He challenges us to speak once again of the penis, a body part completely absent these days in popular books on parenting boys.

This issue of contemporary psychoanalysis, my last as editor-in-chief, embodies the qualities that I and the editorial staff of the journal have sought. We have tried to expand the range of psychoanalytic thinking to include ignored, difficult, or controversial topics, weaving together interpersonal, intrapsychic, and cultural perspectives. We begin this issue with an exploration of psychoanalytic work by Mary Brady with a gay teenager, as she struggled to escape the shackles of disinformation she had acquired during her training and find a fresh approach. We continue this theme with Chana Ullman's description of her work with a gay man, also analyzing the effect of her personal values and the cultural unconscious, with an interesting sidelight on disguise and confidentiality. Abby Stein provides an insightful analysis of counter-transferential and public reactions to sex offenders, with startling facts about how leniently the law treats intrafamilial incest. Steven Tublin explores the dilemma of how to conduct a treatment within the paradoxical confinement of postmodern not-knowingness. That is followed by an interview with Bruce Fink that is a “guide for the perplexed” about Lacan. Finally, there is a series of articles on how Interpersonal psychoanalysis has shaped contemporary approaches to clinical issues.

During my years as editor, I have tried to include articles that other journals avoided. It is easy to publish articles that describe treatments that work out happily, and there is no shortage of them. But we have published articles by psychoanalysts who were also patients in which the analytic process went awry: an analyst who severely broke confidentiality and refused to acknowledge responsibility for it (Burka, 2008), and an analyst who crossed a sexual boundary with a patient and never discussed it with her (Dimen, 2011). Both articles generated enormous discussion. If psychoanalysts do not speak up about misconduct in our field, who will? And if no one will speak about it, how can we learn from our mistakes and endeavor to correct them?

Let me begin by saying that The Monster Within is so good that I had a hard time figuring out what to say about it. It is a compassionate, clearly written book dealing with the topic of maternal ambivalence, which is as universal as sibling rivalry (or, some would say, the Oedipus complex), if less universally acknowledged. The author, Barbara Almond, addresses this topic using two types of material. The first includes clinical vignettes from her practice, and a few of her own personal family-and friend-related observations; the other uses so-called “case stories”— essentially applied psychoanalysis—in which she uses examples from classic and popular literary works. The concept of this book arose, she writes in her preface, out of her clinical and personal experience as a psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, and mother, and her growing awareness of the ubiquity and importance of the phenomenon of maternal ambivalence and its darker side, whether accepted or denied.

This book had a long gestation, according to Dr. Almond, who was kind enough to speak with me as I prepared to write this review. She conceptualized it as a book directed at nonprofessionals, but it was not welcomed with open arms by the commercial publishing world—in fact, it met with considerable resistance, presumably because of its topic. Ultimately, it was published by an academic press. In fact, I think it is a highly accessible book that welcomes a lay audience into the analytic frame in a warm, nurturing, and, let me say, maternal way. Dr. Almond told me, however, the book has been more popular among the psychoanalytic community than the lay readership for whom it was intended. Although it should have been a runaway bestseller with every literate mother (unsurprisingly, it was not), its warm reception among analysts makes sense. It is extremely enjoyable to read a book that gives such clear, jargon-free definitions of psychoanalytic and psychodynamic terms and ideas. I think Almond's clarity is mainly a function of her preference for unambiguous language.

Psychoanalysis and religion are strange bedfellows. A strong belief in one may rattle our foundation in the other. An evening with my analyst friends reminded me of this uneasy coupling. That Friday night, challah and wine graced our friendship. Bonded together by our shared history in psychoanalysis, we offered news, professional development and then, perhaps incited by institute gossip, we debated about Israel. Now, our comfort with each other threatened, one of us suggested we think instead about our Jewish identity. Oddly, though all of us are Jewish, the very personal nature of this question, the depth and enormity of it, silenced us as we each retreated to ponder: What is our Jewish identity?

Freud, absorbed as he was with psychoanalytic discovery, grappled with the question of his Jewish identity throughout his life, as is made clear in the collection of essays The Jewish World of Sigmund Freud: Essays on Cultural Roots and the Problem of Religious Identity. Through an examination of his theories, autobiographical information, dreams, letters, and tidbits, the authors of these essays reveal the complexity of this issue for Freud. Like his theories, Freud's views on his Judaism at times contradict each other, at others elude us. The quotes cited in this book illustrate that towards his Judaism, Freud is fiercely devoted, on the one hand, and dismissive, on the other. Freud, in his inimitable way, has left us to do with his Judaism what he has left us to do with his theories: to delve, examine, question, argue, and posture, which, in Talmudic fashion, the authors of these essays do. To those interested in his Jewish identity, Freud left the body of information that made up his life for us to discover what his Jewish identity was.

As Salberg tells us in her essay, Freud's dreams and theories uncover aspects of Freud's Judaism that remain largely hidden. As Freud grew up, his parents began to assimilate to the Viennese culture, while maintaining Jewish heritage.

The Interpersonal school has been on the cutting edge of progressive thinking about sexuality. Harry Stack Sullivan, with his ward for gay schizophrenics, showed the curative value of protecting a psychotic patient from stigma and prejudice. Edwin Weinstein showed that cultural norms shape paranoid delusions, questioning the traditional Freudian connection of paranoia and homosexuality. Sullivan and contemporary Interpersonalists have tried to disconnect judgments of sexual psychopathology from cultural and religious norms, seeking instead to help people find ways of achieving a satisfactory sexual life without undue anxiety and loss of self-esteem. A key factor in maintaining a progressive outlook on sexuality is to welcome people with nontraditional sexuality and gender identification into the psychoanalytic community.

Theory is usually given short shrift in the literature geared towards college mental health professionals. Pragmatic writings on how to deal with various problems and crises tend to be favored instead—and arguably for good reason. In a recent national survey of university counseling center directors (Gallagher, 2010), 91% reported that the number of students with severe psychological problems continues to climb. Tragedies involving shooting rampages by college students, such as those that have taken place at Columbine, Colorado, Virginia Tech, and most recently, Tucson, Arizona, occur with shocking frequency, raising questions about the ability of university counseling centers to monitor unstable students and prevent harm. Media coverage of campus suicides and overextended counseling center staff (Gabriel, 2010) has also raised awareness of the fact that outreach and triage are crucial to the functioning of university mental health centers.

It is, nonetheless, a wonder how little is written in the psychoanalytic literature about working with college students. The one book devoted to the topic (May 1988) was published almost a quarter century ago. Recent books on college mental health tend to be edited works in which material is organized by topic such as substance abuse or eating disorders (e.g., Grayson & Meilman, 2006), or solution-focused books written for the parent or layperson (e.g., Kadison & DiGeronimo, 2004). A few articles have been published in psychoanalytic journals recently (e.g., Hart, 2003; Kline, 2006), but peer-reviewed journals of the university mental health profession rarely publish psychoanalytically oriented articles. This dearth may reflect a widespread falling out of favor of psychoanalytic thought among mental health professionals. It is more likely, however, to be due to the fact that psychodynamic or psychoanalytic treatment is generally thought of as a long-term modality, whereas college counseling usually is based on a short-term model.

In this remarkable offering of probing and enlightening studies, editors Lewis Aron and Libby Henik make the bold claim that they have gathered, “for the first time in the English language,” an investigation of the mutual relevance and influence of current psychoanalytic theory and the Jewish interpretive tradition. The bridging of psychoanalysis and Judaism is not new, but it has not been attempted in the decades since the explosion of theorizing of the post-classical psychoanalytic turn. Certainly, posing the question of what is to be gained by such a juxtaposition is valuable in and of itself—this volume is proof enough of that. The importance of the analyst's subjectivity, the contribution of cultural factors on the psychoanalytic enterprise, and the hermeneutic perspective all come across dramatically.

All of the authors have made an invaluable contribution in the volume's open ended, the-question's-the-thing spirit. To the mind of this reviewer, even if the idea that psychoanalysis' origins in the Jewish minds of the 19th and 20th centuries might have suggested such, it is now clear that the field of psychoanalysis is its own body of theory and practice, owned by no religious, cultural, or social group. These three excellent articles by Irwin Hirsch, Christopher Bonovitz, and Mark Blechner on the impact of the Interpersonal tradition on contemporary psychoanalytic thinking illuminate different aspects of the Interpersonal tradition. They may, however, inadvertently demonstrate the hermeneutical difficulty inherent in engaging the past with the lexicon of the present. Something gets lost in translation, not just between languages, but also over the passage of time. Subtle slippages in the meaning of words, and more important, in the underlying paradigms, ensue. Reading this fascinating book by the former managing director of The Analytic Press, I had the recurrent image of being under water, looking up. It was impossible, of course, to see beyond the mirrored surface, but the objects at the surface, outlined with brilliant light, were startlingly clear: half-submerged, swimming bodies, the hulls of boats, the bottoms of surfboards and rubber rafts, floating leaves, the piles of piers lapped by waves, resting sea birds. It was a strange disorienting perspective, yet undoubtedly real and thoroughly compelling.

Paul Stepansky has done an extraordinary job of reflecting our world back to us, but upside-down, as it were, inside-out. It's not the picture we usually see, cluttered with our conventional notions of what we expect to encounter. Moreover, it is a somewhat idiosyncratic view, colored by his unique experiences in the field, as a publisher, historian of psychiatry and medicine, and editor of a wide spectrum of psychoanalytic authors. But it is brilliant and true—and deeply felt. His book offers a unique opportunity to see ourselves as, I believe, we need to see ourselves today: a professional world fragmented, marginalized, incoherent, and fading.

Resistance, change in psychoanalysis, relational unconscious, social unconscious

This article describes the fear of metamorphosis in analysis as a relational dynamic, and as a particular form of resistance to change that may lie at the heart of clinical impasses. The fear of metamorphosis is the patient's fear of a complete alteration of valued aspects of her or his self-hood, which she or he experiences as an imminent catastrophe. This fear of metamorphosis is understood here as the analysand's attempt to protect aspects of her or his self-hood from transformation, especially vis-à-vis the analyst's “otherness,” and the impasses that may ensue, reflecting the analyst's and the patient's coconstruction of this otherness. I will examine the dialectics of wishing for transformation and the fear of it. This presents an inherent paradox that may emerge in the clinical encounter as a mutual unspoken and unformulated demand affecting both patient and analyst. I argue that the fear of metamorphosis is a particular variation of the resistance to change. Drawing on Bromberg's (1998) reformulation of resistance as “staying the same while changing,” I reexamine the clinical significance of this fear in the context of traditional and contemporary definitions of resistance, illustrated with a clinical example.

In the clinical literature, the term “parallel process” describes the way in which the dynamics of supervision echo those taking place in the relationship between the therapist and the patient. Gray and Fiscalini (1987) discerned how the same kind of unconscious enactments could occur in any sequence of interpersonal engagements that shared similar characteristics. Sex offenders, forensic practitioners, representatives of the criminal justice system, and the public embody such a dynamic series. Their parallel identifications often drive communal enactments that fuel misguided social policies regarding sex crimes. In this article, I examine how the deep splitting triggered by our own sexual desires and fears has fueled a contemporary hysteria that vilifies strangers, who may not have even committed any serious crimes, while deflecting attention from the most frequent location of sexual offense: the home.

Wilhelm Reich, free clinics, letters of Sigmund Freud, history of psychoanalysis

Wilhelm Reich was a leading thinker of the second generation of psychoanalysts after Freud and, though arguably its most original theorist, always its most controversial. In a series of 10 letters (archived in the U.S. Library of Congress) that span the years 1924 through 1930, Reich and Freud respond to a unique worldview, a specific fusion of activist politics and psychoanalysis. Reich treated workers, farmers, students, maids, soldiers, and bureaucrats at the Ambulatorium, the free psychoanalytic clinic in Vienna of which he was the assistant director. There he realized how vitally individuals are inseparable from their social environments. Like an analysis which frees the individual from inner oppression and releases the flow of natural energies, so—Reich believed—the political left would free the oppressed and release their innate, self-regulating social equanimity. And in these letters, we find the depth with which Freud agreed.

aesthetic conflict, primitive love, transference-love

One of the essential elements in psychoanalysis, promoting growth of the mind, is the analyst's capacity to contain the pain of the aesthetic conflict (Meltzer, 1988) and bear the patient's primitive, often adhesive, dependent and ruthless love. The aesthetic conflict emerges in the presence of the love object and not in its absence. Mental pain seems to overwhelm the patient/infant as he is confronted by the fact that the love object, arousing an ecstatic and sublime sense of oneness is also enigmatic, ambiguous, separate, and outside his omnipotent control. This overflow of ecstasy and the pain of impending separateness can only be borne if adequately contained by the object herself. When the object is experienced as inaccessible to this primitive love, the patient/infant may recoil into autistic encapsulation, or try to penetrate forcefully through intrusive identification. The dialectic interplay between primitive love, idealization, and mature love is stressed, and illustrated in the analyses of two male patients.

Among violent criminal offenders, contemptuous feelings toward others—often in response to real or imagined humiliations—often provide an internal justification for senseless acts of brutality. In my forensic work, I have understood contempt—and other so called “negative emotions”—as part of the constellation of dissociated affects and consequent defenses that fuel dire enactments.

However, inspired by my work with a private client, I have begun to recognize the potential value of negative affects as a way of freeing women from their enmeshment with brutal partners. In this article I examine the moral and interpersonal consequences of the range of contemptuous thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Through the lens of feminist philosophy and interpersonal psychoanalysis, I suggest ways that such feelings might be liberated from destructive intentions, and repurposed as a catalyst for empowerment and change.

In Memoriam: Alberta Szalita, M.D.

1910-2010

Alberta Szalita, M.D., who died on November 10, 2010 at the age of 100, was one of the great psychoanalysts of the twentieth century. She received her M.D. from the University of Warsaw and practiced at first as a neurologist. After losing most of her family during the Holocaust, Szalita came to the United States, met Frieda Fromm-Reichmann, and embarked on analytic training. She worked at Chestnut Lodge from 1949 to 1953, where she demonstrated an extraordinary ability to communicate with psychotic patients. Clara Thompson invited her to join the faculty of the William Alanson White Institute, where she taught for five decades, as well as at the Columbia Psychoanalytic Center. Fluent in many languages, she also pioneered psychoanalytic psychotherapy training programs in Israel and Norway.

Szalita's influence was profound. She was the master of the one-liner. Both patients and supervisees were astonished at her ability to sum up the clinical situation in a short sentence and then pursue that insight until it was understood and integrated. Her papers were laconic and to the point. She was often far ahead of her time in developing highly original ideas. For example, she argued (Szalita, 1958/2001) that dissociation between “ego islands” was central to psychopathology, and that a clinician could help a patient by reconnecting those split-off ego islands through a process that she called “psychointegration.” In recent decades, that approach to treatment has become widely adopted (e.g., Davies & Frawley, 1992; Bromberg, 1998). She also argued strongly for integrating family interviewing with individual treatment (Szalita, 1968, 1970) and for an “epistemological approach” to delusions and hallucinations that prefigured the approach of Kernberg (1984). During the time that some psychoanalysts were attributing schizophrenia to faulty mothering, Szalita (1964, 1968) argued that schizophrenia is not caused by family dynamics.

Therapeutic attachment can help a college-aged woman deal with separation from her mother, making the transition from dependence to mutually supportive peer relationships. An insecure relationship experience with the mother replays in treatment as a patient resists therapeutic influence. Serving as a secure base, a therapist can help a young woman let go of potentially self-fulfilling negative expectations and develop trust that she can find responsive caregiving, internalizing a capacity to love and be loved. Using two case examples that illustrate different attachment styles, one anxious and the other avoidant, I explore my struggle to deal with the injury of feeling discounted while seeking opportunities for connection. Examining our interaction, I consider the patient's and my own role in perpetuating patterns of insecure attachment. By helping a young woman to better understand her mother as a separate person and to express autonomy within the treatment relationship, therapists can foster healthier attachments while supporting individuation.

Pascal Sauvayre   Member of the faculty and a supervising analyst at the William Alanson White Institute. He is a member of the editorial board of Contemporary Psychoanalysis and has a private practice in New York City.

Reading lacan is an experience, not necessarily a pleasant one, but one not to be dismissed. For example, I read the sentence in front of me, and it seems to make sense, but I am often unable to connect it to the sentence before or after, and I feel lost, confused, disoriented. I imagine it is like trying to find one's way in a cavern with just a small lighter that illuminates only the immediate space in front of you, leaving you plunged in the vast darkness of the mind.

We would surely prefer to avoid such experiences, or to have these caverns landscaped and appropriately lit (with clear theory guides) to accommodate our visits to such depths and to make them pleasant. Indeed, we devote much of our mental energy and resources to this sort of landscaping and construction in order to obtain as coherent a “reality” (or psychic reality) as possible. Lacan devoted his efforts to unmasking perceived reality's thin cover of imaginary coherence to reveal its real inaccessibility.

Lacan's writings and his style of theorizing take us down the kind of rabbit holes he believes constitute the psyche. To an American sensibility, all this can seem needlessly convoluted, impractical, and, ultimately, useless. But Bruce Fink has devoted his career to introducing, translating, and interpreting Lacan to the American psychoanalytic community. With a bicultural analytic education, he has helped us to appreciate the French preoccupation with the aesthetics of thought, which is often reduced to an arrogant dismissal of American practicality. Fink has made it his mission to familiarize us with a different analytic language, and thereby draw our attention to our blind spots to Freud, or to what Lacan, and a whole tradition, would claim to be the true Freud. Because of widely differing perspectives on the foundations of psychoanalysis, Fink forces us to consider again the very soul of psychoanalysis, and to question our self-concept as psychoanalysts.

How and when to bring a psychoanalysis to a meaningful, growth-producing close is an issue that has received far too little attention. As psychoanalysis has increasingly focused on therapeutic process rather than metatheory, exploring the neglected process of termination seems crucial. Good Enough Endings, an edited volume by Jill Salberg, attempts to fill this void. Motivated both by her students' reactions to clinical material she presented about a patient who felt “kicked out of therapy,” and by her own less-than-smooth termination process with her analyst, Salberg began studying termination and writing about it herself. Ultimately, she decided to take on the project of creating a book that would describe contemporary Relational perspectives on termination and other endings in psychoanalytic work. The final product includes a wealth of clinical wisdom about this tender and vulnerable period in analysis. I suspect that readers will recognize the dilemmas and challenges that the writers of the various chapters faced as they worked towards ending relationships that were precious both to them and to their patients.

The experiences and struggles involved in graduating from psychoanalytic training and then beginning a private practice are rarely discussed in depth. The influences of the analyst's social class, economic history, and financial circumstances are rarely mentioned, even though they can have a significant impact on how well one does financially. The profession has been mostly silent on the ramifications of the “job” aspects of the psychoanalytic profession. Practicing psychoanalysis will always be a difficult undertaking, yet this hardship is largely ignored during analytic training and the building of a psychoanalytic private practice remains a mystery. Relational models of treatment rely on increased openness and the exploration of all aspects of emotional life. In this spirit, a discussion on how we feel about our level of financial success relative to each other should be acceptable.

Relational theorists have been reluctant to codify technical principles, advocating instead a broad menu of sanctioned interventions and considerable freedom in the analytic moment. This stance, however, conflicts with the need for structure and discipline, which are necessary to conduct a coherent and purposeful analytic treatment. The attempts by four influential Relational theorists to resolve this tension are reviewed, as is the role of implicit community norms in shaping analytic conduct. A conceptualization of Relational technique, resting on the notion of therapeutic intent rather than on the antiquated criterion of objective correctness, is proposed.

The author explores the role of the body and bodily experience in emerging from mental paralysis and a sense of annihilation. Evidence of the body and the working through of bodily sensations can offer the analysand proof of his or her subjective dimension. Two clinical cases are presented: a case of infertility that developed in an unforeseen way and a case of so-called erotic transference in which bodily manifestations of erotic feelings opened the way to the analysand's discovery of her own body and her personal world of affects. Sexual boundary violations are as old as psychoanalysis itself. Yet, although this professional, intellectual, clinical, and personal dilemma is receiving more attention in the literature, it endures. Do analysts not want to think or talk about it? Is our shared shame, or even ambivalence, in the way? Is the primal crime inherently unstoppable? The author examines her own experience of a sexual boundary violation from clinical and theoretical perspectives. Locating her analyst's transgression in its 1970s cultural history, the article attempts to decipher what led up to it: What did the analyst do and not do, say and not say? How did the analyst's character combust with her author's to produce a conflagration about which the analyst never spoke and the author/patient remained silent for thirty years? And under what circumstances can the damage inflicted by such an ethical lapse be transformed?

This historical-theoretical article reviews prewar efforts at a “Marx-Freud synthesis,” stressing the rejection among socialist psychoanalysts of Freud's death-instinct theory. It then considers a second form of synthesis that was developed after World War II: a practical synthesis focused on meeting the needs of children and families traumatized during the War that would work through social democratic state programs and services in which psychoanalytic research on child development would be key. But psychoanalytic contributions were less influential as postwar theorists explored both the origins of war and the nature of prejudices—a topic that once again became crucial as European social democracies were challenged in the 1980s with internal inequality, strife, and prejudice against immigrants. The article raises questions about what currently needs to be done theoretically both to continue the postwar exploration of developmental needs and to extend work on prejudices.

The Intersection of the Psychoanalytic Project and religion is hardly new, and can be traced back to Freud's writing desk in Vienna. The Bible and its multitude of characters—indeed its putative Author—have been the subject of countless articles and books. But few have been as challenging or rich as this one. Avivah Zornberg invites us to bring psychoanalytic sophistication of the highest order to an exploration

141

of this foundational text of the Jewish and Christian religious traditions. She writes from a specifically Jewish perspective, but her insights are rewarding for people of all faiths and none.

From its beginnings, Jewish tradition has understood itself, enacted its evolution, and made sense of the world through the process of commentary on its foundational text, the Hebrew Bible. Through her wide-ranging efforts as a public expositor and interpreter of the text, and her two enthusiastically received previous books, The Beginnings of Desire and The Particulars of Rapture, Avivah Zornberg has come to occupy an honored place among contemporary Biblical commentators. In her latest book, Zornberg undertakes a variation on the work for which she has already won acclaim. Its specific objective is to articulate the connections between aspects of the ancient text and facets of the psychoanalytic project.

Zornberg's approach is not historical and only minimally theological. The book focuses on the intrapsychic realities of various figures in Biblical narratives as elaborated by the Midrash—the rabbis' traditional narrative commentary—and of the Bible itself. The objective of this project is to explore the juncture of the human emotional experience with her reconfiguration of the Hebrew Bible. It discusses issues of communication (or its absence), and unconscious processes reflected in Biblical narrative. She explores such issues as the silence of Noah, the traumatic neurosis of Jonah, and psychic implications of the blindness of Isaac. It addresses such subjects as Abraham, the “winner of souls”; transferential love; the binding of Isaac as Abraham's compulsive act necessary to resolve the repressed memory of his own childhood trauma;1 and fleshing out the psychic condition of figures such as Rebecca (Zornberg finds layers of meanings in her question, commonly rendered as “if so why do I exist?,” which Zornberg compellingly renders as “Why I?”). At times, Murmuring Deep treats the Biblical text as the product of unconscious processes, seeking in the document clues to the sublimated, repressed material latent in it.

How does the supervisor's presence in the background of the clinical work alter the mode of participation and mutuality being worked out between patient and analyst? And how much more complex does the picture become when, as often occurs in analytic training, the candidate has more than one supervisor on the same case at various points in the treatment? This article chronicles the experience of the author over the course of treatment with her analytic control case, and describes the impact of having a different supervisor each year, exposing the analyst and patient to a range of theoretical and participatory influences. The evolution of a sadomasochistic dynamic within the treatment is presented, along with possible parallel struggles around submission and the search for authenticity for the candidate within the various supervisory relationships. Implications for the development of the candidate's emerging analytic identity will be highlighted.
